newsitem.title: UK: BA, American come under fresh fire.
newsitem.headline: BA, American come under fresh fire.

text.p: British Airways and American Airlines came under fresh attack in Britain Thursday as they prepared to formally apply for approval of their controversial alliance plan in the United States.

Continental Airlines and United Airlines both called on the competition authorities in Britain to toughen up proposed conditions for approving the deal, and in particular said BA should give up more runway slots at London Heathrow.

They both said they did not believe conditions being discussed by Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) would go far enough to allow rivals to mount effective competition to a BA/American combine on transatlantic routes.

The core OFT proposal is that BA and American release a total of 168 weekly takeoff and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport to allow in new competition -- sufficient slots for 12 new daily return services.

But Continental said in comments due to be submitted to the OFT tomorrow that it would require 20 takeoff and landing slots a day at Heathrow along with adequate ground handling facilities if it was to be able to mount effective competition on routes to New York and to Houston.

Otherwise, Continental said, the BA/American alliance would strangle competition on transatlantic routes, controlling more than 60 percent of all seats on the UK/U.S. market and more than 70 percent of seats from Heathrow to the United States.
Chairman Gordon Bethune called the alliance between BA and American effectively the world's largest airline merger.
"BA and AA promise to deliver the ultimate transportation benefit but...this huge deal is as attractive to travellers as that last great wonder of the Atlantic, The Titanic," he said.

United, which unlike Continental already has an operation at Heathrow, said that it was telling the OFT that BA and American should give up more slots at Heathrow and that it should give them up for free.
"BA and American rather than the competing airlines, must pay the economic price for reducing competition in key markets," United said in a statement.

United said it was proposing to the OFT that BA and American should hand over sufficient slots to allow the introduction of 15 new daily trans-Atlantic flights by other airlines -- equivalent to 210 weekly takeoff and landing slots.

Meanwhile industry sources said BA and American were expected to get the ball rolling on the approvals process in the U.S. on Friday by making a joint filing with the departments of Justice and Transportation requesting clearance under U.S. antitrust laws.
The airlines thenmselves said they planned to hold a news conference in Washington Friday to make "an important announcement" but declined to comment further.
